items.method: narrative review of statistical and machine learning fraud detection tools
items.finding: Statistics and machine learning provide effective technologies for fraud detection, applied to money laundering, credit card fraud, telecommunications fraud and computer intrusion. The paper describes available tools and the areas where they are most used.
items.limitations: General fraud domains, not external audit; 2002 review; abstract gives no review method or accuracy figures

items.method: archival empirical study of lobbying expenses and fraud detection (hazard model)
items.sample: Large frauds detected 1998-2004; corporate lobbying data
items.finding: Lobbying firms have a significantly lower hazard of fraud detection, evade detection 117 days longer, and are 38% less likely to be detected by regulators. Fraudulent firms spend 77% more on lobbying than nonfraudulent firms.
items.limitations: Not about AI or auditing technology; concerns regulator detection and political influence

items.method: archival analysis of resume data on AI workers plus interviews with 17 audit partners
items.sample: 310,000+ resumes for 36 largest audit firms; 17 audit partners
items.finding: Greater AI investment by audit firms is associated with improved audit quality, lower fees, and displacement of human auditors. A one-SD increase in AI investment is linked to a 5.0% lower restatement likelihood, 0.9% lower audit fees, and 3.6% (three years) to 7.1% (four years) fewer accounting employees.
items.limitations: AI investment proxied by AI hiring; observational, so causal inference is limited; abstract truncated

items.method: archival empirical study
items.sample: Clients with internal control audits; restatements used as a proxy for material weaknesses
items.finding: Greater audit committee accounting expertise is associated with more adverse internal control opinions among clients with likely weaknesses. It is also associated with a lower likelihood of auditor dismissal after adverse opinions.
items.limitations: Not about AI; concerns audit committee governance and auditor reporting

items.method: archival empirical study of auditor appointments
items.finding: Companies appoint officers' former audit firms more often than alternatives, but less often when audit committees are more independent. This suggests independent audit committees strengthen audit quality by deterring auditor-officer affiliations.
items.limitations: Not about AI; audit quality inferred indirectly from governance; sample not stated in abstract

items.method: conceptual paper proposing an approach
items.finding: The paper presents an approach for applying audit data analytics and machine learning to full population testing instead of sampling, and discusses related challenges.
items.limitations: No empirical evaluation stated in abstract; no quantified effects on quality or cost

items.method: content analysis of Big Four machine learning tools
items.sample: Machine learning tools and platforms of the Big Four firms
items.finding: Big Four firms have developed ML tools for audit coordination, automated audits in limited areas such as cash, data analysis, risk assessment and document extraction. The paper flags ethical, security and privacy-regulation risks.
items.limitations: Descriptive; relies on public information about firm tools; no outcome measures

items.method: panel regression (OLS) with propensity score robustness checks
items.sample: 2,912 non-financial firm-year observations, GCC listed firms, 2010-2023
items.finding: The study examines whether firm AI adoption improves integrated financial reporting, with audit quality (fees, industry specialization, restatement) as a moderator. The abstract is truncated before results.
items.limitations: Concerns client AI adoption and integrated reporting, not auditor AI use; results not visible in the abstract; GCC only

items.method: archival study with propensity score matching and two-stage OLS
items.sample: Chinese firms, 2011-2020
items.finding: When audit firms and clients use AI separately, audit report lag increases. When they use AI together, report lag falls, improving efficiency. AI use is also associated with a lower likelihood of restatement, and the quality link is driven by audit effort lag.
items.limitations: Proxies (report lag, restatement) are indirect; single country; observational

items.method: two experiments with experienced external reviewers
items.sample: Experienced external reviewers (size not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Reviewers rate data and analytics audit procedures as lower quality than traditional ones because they perceive them as less effortful, even at equal assurance. A theory-based intervention reduces reliance on this effort heuristic.
items.limitations: Experimental vignettes; about D&A rather than AI anomaly detection; sample size not given in abstract

items.method: archival empirical study (regression analysis of audit fees, audit hours and audit quality proxies)
items.sample: public firms in the Korean audit market
items.finding: Abnormally low audit fees are associated with larger discretionary accruals and a higher likelihood of meeting or beating analyst forecasts. No significant association was found for abnormally high fees, and the low-fee effect persists regardless of audit hours.
items.limitations: Does not examine AI or analytics; relevant only as an adjacent link between fees, effort and audit quality; single-country setting.

items.method: theoretical framework / conceptual paper drawing on extant literature
items.finding: Proposes a framework for applying ML and data analytics across the internal audit lifecycle, from planning to reporting. It argues auditors need a continuous innovation mindset and effective guardrails.
items.limitations: Conceptual, no empirical test; concerns internal rather than external audit; abstract truncated.

items.method: state-of-the-art literature review of big data challenges and analytics methods
items.finding: Reviews big data challenges and analytics methods that organizations use to support investment decisions. It is general to business and not specific to auditing.
items.limitations: Not audit-specific; no audit quality or cost outcomes.

items.method: literature review of big data techniques in auditing, accounting and finance research
items.finding: Finds that big data techniques are less widespread in auditing than in related fields such as financial fraud modelling. The authors refute the argument that auditors lag because clients use less advanced techniques, and they outline future opportunities.
items.limitations: Review method and scope not detailed in the abstract; does not directly measure audit quality or cost effects.

items.method: desk study / theoretical discussion
items.finding: Argues that COVID-19 social distancing could affect audit fees, effort, procedures and audit quality. It recommends that audit firms invest in digital programs, including AI.
items.limitations: Theoretical and speculative; no empirical data; AI mentioned only as a recommendation.

items.method: semi-structured interviews n=22 plus document analysis
items.sample: 22 individuals experienced in developing, implementing or assessing big data analytics in auditing
items.finding: Provides an overview of how big data and analytics change audit practice, covering auditor-client relationships, engagement conduct and challenges in embedding BDA. It sets out a research agenda.
items.limitations: Qualitative with a small sample; no quantified effects on audit quality or fees; abstract gives no specific results.

items.method: survey / literature review of smart grid big data technologies
items.finding: Surveys big data analytics technologies and challenges in smart grids. It is unrelated to auditing.
items.limitations: Off-topic domain (energy).

items.method: narrative review of heterogeneous data and big data analytics methods
items.finding: Introduces data processing methods, tools and ML/deep learning approaches for heterogeneous big data. It does not address auditing.
items.limitations: Generic technical overview; no audit context; no stated review method.

items.method: archival regression study of audit fees and book-tax differences
items.finding: Book-tax differences are positively associated with audit fees, and the association is larger for firms that appear to have managed earnings. This is consistent with fees reflecting auditor risk assessment and effort.
items.limitations: Does not involve AI or analytics; sample details not given in the abstract; useful only as background on fee determinants.

items.method: archival cross-sectional regression
items.sample: 624 Australian companies, 2011
items.finding: Female audit committee representation is positively associated with audit fees, and it moderates the effects of firm size, risk and complexity on fees. It does not address AI.
items.limitations: Single year, single country; unrelated to AI adoption; audit fees treated as a quality proxy.

items.method: archival regression study (details unclear from abstract)
items.finding: Audit fees are negatively associated with the proportion of long-tenure directors on independent audit committees, consistent with lower audit effort. The study does not examine AI or analytics.
items.limitations: Not about AI or analytics; sample not stated in abstract; association only.

items.method: ISM-DEMATEL-Fuzzy MICMAC barrier modeling
items.sample: Indian manufacturing supply chains; twelve barriers
items.finding: Lack of top management support, financial support, skills, and techniques/procedures are the most significant barriers to big data analytics implementation in Indian manufacturing supply chains.
items.limitations: Supply chain context, not auditing; expert-judgment-based modeling; sample size not stated in abstract.

items.method: conceptual/ethical discussion paper
items.finding: Discusses ethical impacts of big data analytics in infectious disease contexts, including algorithmic reliance, informed consent complexity, and profiling.
items.limitations: Healthcare domain, off-topic for auditing; no empirical data.

items.method: comparative empirical evaluation of 19 unsupervised anomaly detection algorithms on 10 datasets
items.sample: 10 datasets from multiple application domains
items.finding: Evaluates strengths and weaknesses of 19 unsupervised anomaly detection algorithms across datasets, including performance and computational effort. Fraud detection is mentioned only as one application area.
items.limitations: Generic multivariate benchmarks, not audit or journal-entry data.

items.method: benchmarking of 10 supervised and unsupervised ML algorithms on the CICIDS2017 dataset, plus literature review
items.sample: CICIDS2017 network intrusion dataset
items.finding: Benchmarks ML algorithms for anomaly-based intrusion detection to identify suitable algorithms, parameters, and testing criteria.
items.limitations: Network intrusion domain, not financial or audit transactions.

items.method: systematic literature review (Kitchenham) of 93 articles
items.sample: 93 articles
items.finding: Synthesizes ML techniques, fraud types, and evaluation metrics in ML-based financial fraud detection, noting that conventional manual methods are imprecise, costly, and time consuming.
items.limitations: Broad financial fraud (not specifically external audit); review of detection methods, with no measurement of audit quality or costs.

items.method: empirical comparison of six statistical and ML models for financial statement fraud detection
items.sample: fraud and nonfraud firms; 42 predictors examined (sample size not stated)
items.finding: Logistic regression and support vector machines perform well relative to ANN, bagging, C4.5, and stacking at detecting financial statement fraud. Only six of 42 predictors, including discretionary accruals and auditor turnover, are consistently selected.
items.limitations: Firm-level fraud prediction rather than auditor adoption of AI; sample size not stated in abstract.

items.method: review of deep learning in smart grids with bibliometric analysis
items.finding: Reviews deep learning advances and enabling technologies in smart grid systems.
items.limitations: Off-topic energy domain.

items.method: systematic literature review (Kitchenham) of 47 articles
items.sample: 47 articles
items.finding: Reviews ML and data mining methods and datasets for detecting fraudulent financial statements, noting that supervised algorithms are used more than unsupervised ones. Identifies gaps and limitations and suggests future research.
items.limitations: Focus on financial statement fraud detection methods, not auditor adoption or audit outcomes.

items.method: empirical ML experiment: 7 supervised and 2 unsupervised models (isolation forest, autoencoders) on a real-life general ledger dataset
items.sample: one real-life general ledger dataset (size not stated in abstract)
items.finding: The best supervised and unsupervised models show high potential for detecting predefined anomalies in general ledger journal entries, addressing sampling risk and audit inefficiency.
items.limitations: Single dataset; detection of predefined anomalies rather than real-world audit outcomes; no measurement of costs or quality.

items.method: applied case study using cluster analysis on insurance claims data
items.sample: group life insurance claims (size not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Cluster analysis grouped similar claims and flagged small-population clusters for further investigation, helping auditors focus effort. Flagged clusters were characterized by large beneficiary payments, large interest payments and long lag between submission and payment.
items.limitations: Single insurance claims setting; no reported detection accuracy or validation against known fraud; not external audit financial statement data

items.method: deep learning model development combining numerical and textual (MD&A) features
items.sample: 5130 Chinese listed companies' annual reports
items.finding: Develops a deep learning fraud detection system using financial and non-financial indices plus text features from MD&A to address class imbalance in financial statement fraud. Abstract is truncated and performance results are not shown.
items.limitations: Abstract truncated so results unclear; Chinese listed firms only; not tested in actual audit engagements

items.method: narrative survey / taxonomy of deep learning for social media analytics
items.finding: Summarizes deep learning architectures for social media analytics and highlights challenges such as scalability, heterogeneity and multimodality. Not related to auditing or fraud detection.
items.limitations: Off-topic; no stated review methodology

items.method: survey of machine learning methods for video anomaly detection
items.finding: Provides a critical review of recent learning algorithms for anomaly detection in surveillance video, including strengths, weaknesses and anomaly type classifications. Domain is video surveillance, not financial transactions.
items.limitations: Different domain (video); review methodology not described in abstract

items.method: machine learning classifier comparison on benchmark dataset
items.sample: UNSW BoT-IoT dataset
items.finding: Proposes a machine learning-based anomaly detection approach for IoT smart home traffic using four classifiers. Not related to auditing or financial fraud.
items.limitations: Network security domain; results truncated in abstract; benchmark dataset only

items.method: literature review with conceptual model
items.finding: Defines professional skepticism as judgments reflecting heightened assessment of the risk that an assertion is incorrect, and presents a model of how audit evidence combines with auditor knowledge and traits. Notes that excessive skepticism can make audits inefficient and expensive.
items.limitations: Pre-AI (2009) and does not address technology; conceptual rather than empirical

items.method: survey experiment with two scenarios
items.sample: citizens (sample size not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Explainability affects trust in algorithmic decisions more than accessibility, and the effect partly extends to trust in the human decision-maker. Effects are not robust across decision contexts.
items.limitations: Public administration setting with citizens, not auditors; hypothetical scenarios

items.method: two surveys plus interviews with auditors and chief audit executives
items.sample: internal auditors and CAEs (sizes not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Greater use of technology-based audit techniques is associated with more audits completed, more risk factors found, more recommendations and fewer audit days, but also with larger internal audit function size. Interviews indicate benefits are hard to quantify and skilled staff hard to hire.
items.limitations: Internal rather than external audit; perception-based self-report; general audit technology rather than AI specifically

items.method: conceptual framework development (I-TOE) combining UTAUT2 and TOE
items.finding: Proposes an Individual-Technology-Organization-Environment framework to explain adoption of computer-assisted audit techniques by audit firms. The abstract does not report empirical results.
items.limitations: Appears conceptual with no empirical results in abstract; CAATTs rather than AI; dated (2012)

items.method: qualitative study, 44 in-depth interviews
items.sample: 44 auditors, regulators and AI software providers
items.finding: Automating seemingly low-level audit tasks may erode deliberation, sensemaking and reflexivity important for socializing junior auditors, while higher-level audit aspects may be augmented by technology. New technology also creates new areas of indeterminacy.
items.limitations: Qualitative with perception-based data; does not measure audit quality or costs

items.method: cross-sectional questionnaire survey with SEM-PLS (WarpPLS)
items.sample: 91 analyzable questionnaires from auditors in Public Accountant Offices and Ministry of Finance, South Sulawesi, Indonesia
items.finding: Emotional intelligence raises work enthusiasm, spiritual intelligence directly improves auditor performance, and work enthusiasm positively affects auditor performance. The paper does not address AI or anomaly detection.
items.limitations: Small sample, self-report, single region, no AI/technology component

items.method: framing experiment
items.finding: Algorithm aversion becomes more frequent as the consequences of a decision become more serious, which lowers the probability of success in important decisions.
items.limitations: General decision-making context, not auditing; sample size not stated in abstract

items.method: structured questionnaire survey with correlation analysis
items.sample: 169 respondents across sectors in Oman
items.finding: Examines auditors' perceptions of how AI/ML affect professional skepticism and judgment and thereby audit efficiency, including influencing factors and challenges. The abstract is truncated and does not state the results.
items.limitations: Perception-based self-report, single country, focus on internal auditors, correlation only, truncated abstract

items.method: behavioral and questionnaire study
items.sample: in-service and pre-service teachers (size not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Both in-service and pre-service teachers prefer advice from a human counselor over an expert model, and acceptance depends on task difficulty.
items.limitations: Education domain, not auditing; sample size not given in abstract

items.method: online experiment (forecasting task)
items.sample: 1,840 participants
items.finding: Time pressure mitigates algorithm aversion, apparently because forecasters lose confidence in their own forecasts. No support was found for the 'do your best' goals hypothesis, and the abstract is truncated on data input decision rights.
items.limitations: Forecasting/management accounting context rather than external audit; participants likely not auditors

items.method: conceptual overview with guidelines and a digital tool
items.finding: Gives an overview of issues around algorithmic decision support, responsibility and organisational decision-making. It identifies research gaps and proposes guidelines and a tool for mapping responsibility.
items.limitations: Conceptual, no empirical test, not audit-specific

items.method: narrative literature synthesis
items.finding: Synthesizes research on auditor professional skepticism into six attributes (questioning mind, suspension of judgment, search for knowledge, interpersonal understanding, self-esteem, autonomy). It notes that how skepticism is defined and measured remains unclear.
items.limitations: No stated review method; no AI link

items.method: survey/taxonomy of XAI techniques
items.finding: Surveys and classifies XAI techniques and programming frameworks across the machine learning development process.
items.limitations: General AI, not audit-specific; no stated review protocol

items.method: illustrative multiple case studies (3 cases)
items.sample: three government algorithmic decision-making cases
items.finding: Explainable, data-driven decisions are often not perceived as objective by the public and can provoke distrust and resistance. The paper proposes decision-specific strategies to gain acceptance.
items.limitations: Government/public-sector context, not auditing; few illustrative cases

items.method: empirical modelling with Shapley-value explainable AI
items.sample: 15,000 SMEs seeking peer-to-peer lending credit
items.finding: A Shapley-value explainable AI model groups risky and non-risky borrowers by similar financial characteristics, which helps explain credit scores and predict future behavior.
items.limitations: Credit risk in fintech lending, not audit or fraud detection; no performance metrics in abstract

items.method: framework development with real-world case study
items.finding: The paper proposes a framework and overview of techniques to make black-box ML credit scoring models transparent, auditable and explainable. A real-world case study shows comparable interpretability to scorecards can be achieved while retaining predictive power.
items.limitations: Credit scoring context, not external financial statement audit; 'auditable' refers to regulatory model transparency; single case study.

items.method: conceptual overview of RPA ecosystem and challenges (unclear from abstract)
items.finding: The study summarizes the evolving RPA ecosystem and identifies challenges critical for successfully implementing smart (AI-augmented) RPA in accounting and auditing. It notes theoretical frameworks for such deployments are still insufficient.
items.limitations: No empirical method or sample stated in abstract; focuses on RPA rather than anomaly detection; no audit quality or cost outcomes.

items.method: narrative review/editorial
items.finding: The review argues that AI auditing can learn from historical audit practices in financial accounting, safety engineering and the social sciences. It distinguishes among technology-oriented and other approaches to auditing AI systems.
items.limitations: Concerns auditing of AI systems, not use of AI in external financial audits; editorial without stated review method.

items.method: perspective paper based on round-table sessions
items.finding: The paper discusses model risk management for AI/ML models in banks and financial institutions and expects more complex models in anti-money laundering, fraud detection and transaction monitoring. It emphasizes explainable, trustworthy and responsible AI.
items.limitations: Perspective/opinion paper; focus on bank model risk, not external audit; no empirical evidence.

items.method: cross-sectional survey n=143 (technology acceptance model-based)
items.sample: 143 accountants and auditors in companies in Vietnam
items.finding: Technology readiness positively relates to AI adoption among accounting and auditing professionals, with perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use mediating the relationship.
items.limitations: Small sample, single country, self-reported adoption; mixes accountants and auditors; no audit quality or cost outcomes.

items.method: philosophical/conceptual analysis
items.finding: The article identifies three conceptual challenges for interpretable ML: ambiguity of target, disregard for error rates and severe testing, and emphasis on product over process. It argues these can produce misleading explanations.
items.limitations: General ML interpretability theory; no audit context and no empirical data.

items.method: narrative (semi-systematic) literature review, 2015-2020, interpretive/hermeneutic
items.finding: Identifies five major ethical challenges of AI-based decision-making in accounting: objectivity, privacy, transparency, accountability and trustworthiness, structured using Rest's four-component model.
items.limitations: Narrative review with no effect measurement; focused on accounting broadly rather than external audit outcomes; abstract truncated.

items.method: in-depth qualitative case study
items.sample: Big Four audit firms in Japan, 2010s
items.finding: Shows how newly created service R&D organizations advanced AI adoption in external audit services and builds a three-phase model of the process. Addresses organizational adoption rather than audit quality or cost outcomes.
items.limitations: Single-country case study of Big Four firms; no quantitative outcomes on quality or costs.

items.method: narrative review/commentary (method unclear from abstract)
items.finding: Reports that audit firms are keen to use machine learning tools to read contracts, analyze journal entries and assist in fraud detection, and anticipates accelerating adoption.
items.limitations: No stated method or empirical evidence; descriptive and prospective claims only.

items.method: field experiment with multiple regression, n=248
items.sample: 248 auditors from Big4 and non-Big4 firms in Malaysia
items.finding: Professional skepticism and experience positively affect risk-of-misstatement assessment while time budget pressure negatively affects it. Experience strengthens and time pressure weakens the skepticism effect.
items.limitations: Does not involve AI; single-country sample; risk assessment as outcome rather than actual detection.

items.method: cross-sectional survey with PLS, n=173
items.sample: 173 internal auditors at Indonesia's Inspectorate General of the Ministry of Education and Culture
items.finding: Auditor experience and professional skepticism positively affect fraud detection, while competence, independence and time pressure have no direct effect. Skepticism mediates these relationships.
items.limitations: Public-sector internal auditors, not external audit; no AI component; self-reported survey from a single institution.

items.method: qualitative critical review of ongoing debates
items.finding: Explores the role of AI in external auditing and assesses debates, with proponents citing better sampling, efficiency and audit quality and opponents citing ethical concerns, bias, job loss and human-machine coordination challenges.
items.limitations: Review without clear systematic method in the abstract; no empirical measurement of effects; abstract truncated.

items.method: online questionnaire survey with principal axis factor analysis, n=206
items.sample: 206 auditing and accounting practitioners and students in Poland
items.finding: Respondents perceive that AI adoption increases audit efficiency, enhances client communication and service, and automates routine tasks. Three factors explain 62.2% of variance.
items.limitations: Perception-based survey; Poland only; mixes practitioners and students.

items.method: cross-sectional survey with OLS regression, n=125
items.sample: 125 accounting firms in Nigeria applying AI (purposive sample from population of 178)
items.finding: Expert systems, machine learning and intelligent agents showed significant positive relationships with audit quality in Nigeria.
items.limitations: Purposive sampling; self-reported questionnaire; single country; audit quality measured by perception rather than objective outcomes.

items.method: archival regression analysis of audit fees
items.sample: listed U.S. companies, 2016-2021
items.finding: Documents a statistically and economically significant audit fee premium for audit partners with digitalization expertise, strongest in highly digitalized industries and diminishing over time in less digitalized industries.
items.limitations: Measures partner digitalization expertise, not AI anomaly detection directly; U.S. listed firms only.

items.method: survey with moderated regression analysis
items.sample: auditors at public accounting firms in Bali Province, Indonesia, purposive sample
items.finding: Time budget pressure has a negative but statistically non-significant effect on audit quality; audit structure, independence and supervision were examined as moderators.
items.limitations: No AI component; regional sample; perception-based audit quality measure; abstract truncated.

items.method: archival empirical study using novel office-level audit-employee turnover data
items.finding: Audit-employee turnover within accounting firm offices is associated with costlier, less timely, less thorough and lower-quality audits, and leads to greater auditor switching. The effect is stronger when other strains exist in the auditor-client relationship and varies by employee rank and timing.
items.limitations: Does not examine AI or analytics adoption; only indirectly relevant as context on audit cost and quality drivers. Sample size not stated in the abstract.

items.method: narrative literature review / discussion paper
items.finding: Reviews audit research to identify behavioral challenges to professional skepticism when using audit data analytics, from five perspectives: attitudes toward ADA, data characteristics, anomalies identified by ADA, auditor mindsets, and social contexts. It argues that ADA offers benefits but also threatens appropriate skepticism and ultimately audit quality.
items.limitations: No empirical test or systematic review method stated; conceptual discussion focused on ADA broadly rather than AI/ML anomaly detection.

items.method: framework development with ML model comparison (XGBoost vs other algorithms)
items.finding: Proposes a blockchain-based automated insurance framework that uses XGBoost to detect fraudulent claims and assess risk, and compares it with other state-of-the-art algorithms.
items.limitations: Insurance claims setting, not external audit; abstract gives no sample or quantitative results.

items.method: systematic literature review (PRISMA and Kitchenham) of 104 articles, 2012-2023
items.sample: 104 articles
items.finding: Reviews ML techniques for financial fraud detection and notes a trend toward real datasets. Credit card fraud models are the most common application.
items.limitations: Not specific to external audit; abstract is truncated; summarizes the literature without evaluating audit quality or cost.

items.method: literature review of 65 articles on data mining for financial fraud, 2004-2015
items.sample: 65 articles (58 journal, 7 conference)
items.finding: Identifies 41 data mining techniques used across financial fraud applications such as health insurance and credit card. Logistic regression appeared to be the leading tool.
items.limitations: Older literature (2004-2015); not audit-specific; narrative synthesis; abstract truncated.

items.method: empirical comparison of seven fraud prediction models using a cost-based measure
items.sample: firm-level fraud and restatement samples (size not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Even the best models trade off false to true positives at rates above 100:1. The resulting false positives make all seven models too costly for auditors to implement, though M-Score and F-Score give net benefits to investors and several models are viable for regulators.
items.limitations: Tests traditional fraud prediction models rather than modern AI/ML tools; depends on assumptions about cost parameters.

items.method: empirical comparison of seven ML classifiers with SMOTE and undersampling
items.sample: 341 Turkish SMEs, 2013-2017; 1384 non-fraud and 321 fraud cases
items.finding: Evaluates seven ML classifiers for detecting financial accounting fraud in SME financial statements, using sampling methods to handle class imbalance.
items.limitations: Single country, bank-sourced data of SMEs; highly imbalanced classes; results truncated in abstract; not an audit setting.

items.method: supervised ML experiments on the BoT-IoT dataset
items.sample: BoT-IoT dataset
items.finding: Develops an IoT intrusion detection system using a seven-feature set that detects DDoS, DoS, reconnaissance and information theft attacks with supervised ML.
items.limitations: Network security domain, unrelated to auditing or financial fraud.

items.method: ML ensemble modeling with explainable AI on cryptocurrency transactions
items.sample: Ethereum transaction data (size not stated)
items.finding: A hard voting ensemble reached 99% accuracy in detecting fraudulent Ethereum transactions. The authors stress XAI for transparency and trust.
items.limitations: Cryptocurrency context, not external audit; high accuracy may reflect class balance or data issues; no audit outcomes.

items.method: literature survey of 101 articles on ML anomaly detection, 2015-2022
items.sample: 101 articles
items.finding: Surveys ML anomaly detection across system log, network, cloud and medical domains. Most researchers use real-life datasets and unsupervised learning.
items.limitations: Security and IT focus; no financial audit content.

items.method: ML system development and evaluation for network anomaly detection (unsupervised and supervised, with SHAP)
items.sample: network traffic data (size not stated)
items.finding: Random Forest reached 94.3% accuracy in classifying network anomalies. SHAP was used for interpretability.
items.limitations: Network traffic domain, not financial transactions or audit.

items.method: comparison of ML algorithms (RF, NB, SVM, decision tree) for IoT anomaly detection
items.finding: Random Forest performed best, with 99.5% accuracy in detecting anomalies in IoT network data.
items.limitations: IoT security domain, unrelated to auditing; limited methodological detail in abstract.

items.method: comparative empirical study of five bagging- and boosting-based ensemble learning models
items.sample: Chinese A-share listed companies, 2012-2022
items.finding: Bagging outperforms boosting across various evaluation indicators in detecting financial statement fraud. Profitability and asset quality are positively associated with financial fraud.
items.limitations: Abstract gives no sample size or metric values. It does not address audit settings, auditor adoption, audit quality or costs. Single-country data.

items.method: unclear from abstract (autoencoder and deep dense neural network detection model)
items.finding: The paper proposes an approach using autoencoders and deep dense neural networks to detect cryptojacking web threats. The abstract is truncated and gives no results.
items.limitations: Cybersecurity topic, not financial fraud or auditing. Abstract is truncated and reports no performance results.
